title: Is an AI downturn unavoidable?
gist: Oxford Economics says AI-related capex was an estimated 27% of US fixed investment in Q2 and has cumulatively topped 2% of US GDP over three years, a surge exceeded only by 1840s UK railway mania. With utilisation-adjusted productivity growth decelerating and AI firms showing negative free cash flow, it warns consensus profit growth looks inconsistent with likely productivity gains and that a sharp correction risk intensifies into 2027.

themes.theme: Scale of the AI investment boom

insights.claim: AI-related capex accounted for an estimated 27% of US fixed investment in Q2 2026, and cumulative investment in the sector has topped 2% of US GDP over the past three years; among historical tech booms only the 1840s UK railway mania saw a larger investment surge.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: US growth and capex composition are heavily concentrated in one theme, so an AI pullback would hit aggregate investment, not just tech multiples.
insights.quote: AI-related capex accounted for an estimated 27% of US fixed investment in Q2

insights.claim: Most past tech-related booms ended abruptly and often painfully even where the technology delivered strong economic benefits, and that risk looks significant for AI too.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A correct view on AI's long-run value does not protect against a drawdown; the timing risk is separate from the technology thesis.
insights.quote: Most other examples ended abruptly, often painfully, even where the technology delivered strong economic benefits.
insights.locator: The AI boom continues to grow

insights.claim: Evidence of large returns from AI is limited so far: utilisation-adjusted measures of US productivity growth are decelerating, whereas the dotcom boom produced productivity benefits quite quickly, so AI must deliver tangible gains soon, especially as AI firms show negative free cash flow.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The dotcom comparison sets a timing bar: without visible productivity gains soon, negative-FCF AI spenders face a funding and sentiment problem.
insights.quote: the dotcom boom of a quarter of a century ago produced productivity benefits quite quickly
insights.locator: The surge in investment reflects hopes

insights.claim: Current consensus estimates of profit growth in the AI sector look inconsistent with Oxford Economics' own estimates of the likely productivity gains from AI.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Suggests sell-side earnings expectations for AI-linked names embed more than macro productivity can plausibly support, a setup for estimate cuts.
insights.quote: Current consensus estimates of profit growth in the sector look inconsistent with our estimates of the likely productivity gains from AI.
insights.locator: Current consensus estimates of profit growth

insights.claim: A sharp AI-sector correction does not require the technology to prove worthless, only disappointment relative to currently elevated expectations; possible triggers include profitability concerns, negative news on productivity gains and demand, regulatory risks and rising US interest rates, with these risks intensifying as 2027 approaches.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Watch the expectations gap and US rates as catalysts; risk is framed as rising into 2027 rather than imminent.
insights.quote: it doesn’t require the technology to prove worthless, only for there to be disappointment relative to the currently elevated expectations
insights.locator: Importantly, for there to be a sharp correction
